messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Children Present: Being around children, Media / News: Related news, Known People: Related people
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir had spent most of his life working as a roofer, exposed to all sorts of elements and hazards. But it was one particular incident 10 years ago that changed everything for him. He was working on a project when he accidentally inhaled a toxic chemical while applying a new type of sealant. The fumes overwhelmed him, causing him to lose consciousness and fall off the roof. When he came to, his coworkers were frantically calling for an ambulance. As Amir recounts this event, it's clear that the sensory details are still vividly etched in his mind - the smell of the chemicals, the feeling of disorientation, the sound of his colleagues' panicked voices. But what frightens him most is not the memory itself, but how it has become intertwined with his daily life. He can't be around children without being suddenly transported back to that moment, worrying about their safety and his own vulnerability. Even seeing kids playing in a park or watching family movies with his grandkids becomes an ordeal. The media hasn't helped either. Any news report about industrial accidents or chemical spills sends Amir into a tailspin of anxiety. He'll watch the footage, mesmerized by the images of destruction and chaos, unable to shake off the feeling that it could happen again - this time to someone he loves. His wife, Fatima, has noticed how withdrawn Amir becomes after these episodes, how he'll pace around the house, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. People who know about the accident also trigger a reaction in Amir. Coworkers from that fateful day will occasionally reach out, asking how he's doing or reminiscing about old times. But for Amir, their inquiries are like reopening an old wound. He'll become guarded and evasive, unsure of how to respond without unraveling. The physical consequences of the accident have also taken a toll on Amir's life. His startle response has become so pronounced that even a gentle touch from Fatima can send him into a panic. "I'm just resting my hand on your shoulder," she'll say, confused by his reaction. He knows it's irrational, but he can't shake off the feeling of vulnerability. As a result, Amir struggles to relax, even in safe spaces like his own home. His mind is always on high alert, anticipating potential dangers and threats. Sleep has become a luxury he can no longer afford; the memories of that day will creep into his dreams, forcing him awake with a jolt. When he tries to recall what happened deliberately, he finds himself hitting a mental block - as if his brain is trying to protect him from the trauma. But at other times, the memories come flooding back unbidden, like a nightmare he can't wake up from. The most disorienting part for Amir is when emotions overwhelm him without any clear memory or image attached. He'll feel an intense sense of dread or anxiety and won't know why. It's as if his body remembers what happened even when his mind doesn't. This has left him feeling disconnected from himself, unsure of how to navigate these unpredictable mood swings. Lately, Fatima has been urging Amir to seek help. She's noticed how his moods have become increasingly erratic and isolated. The incident 10 years ago was just the beginning; what followed was a decade-long struggle with anxiety, fear, and hypervigilance. As Amir finally begins to confront this reality, he's most afraid of losing himself completely - of becoming so consumed by these memories that he can no longer connect with his loved ones or find peace in his own home. He's hoping that therapy will help him reclaim some semblance of normalcy and learn to live alongside the shadows of that fateful day.
